content: Mercury(II) oxide, also known as mercuric oxide, is a chemical compound with the formula HgO and a molecular weight of 216. The red form of mercury(II) oxide can be synthesized by heating elemental mercury in the presence of oxygen at approximately 350 °C. Alternatively, it can be produced through the pyrolysis of mercury(II) nitrate [Hg(NO3)2]. The yellow form of mercury(II) oxide, on the other hand, can be obtained by precipitating aqueous Hg²⁺ ions with an alkali solution. Mercury(II) oxide has applications in the production of elemental mercury due to its ability to decompose readily. Upon decomposition, it releases oxygen gas. Historically, this property played a significant role in the discovery of oxygen. In 1774, Joseph Priestley observed the release of a gas when heating mercuric oxide, which he referred to as dephlogisticated air based on the prevailing phlogiston theory of the time. Later, Antoine Lavoisier identified this gas as oxygen, naming it after its ability to form acidic compounds. This historical event is often cited as a major milestone in the field of chemistry, although the attribution of the discovery of oxygen remains a subject of debate. Additionally, mercury(II) oxide is utilized as a material for cathodes in mercury batteries.
